name: Bagirmi
catalog_quote: 2° Lorsqu'un mot se trouve dans l'intérieur de la proposition, ou d'un mot composé, ou s'il comporte un suffixe, si l'accent ne porte pas sur sa voyelle finale, cette voyelle disparaît. Ce sont ces mots dont nous séparons la voyelle finale par le signe /. Si, au contraire, l'accent porte sur la voyelle finale, le mot ne subit aucune altération.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation (Gaden 1909:9, Lois phonétiques 2°) is present verbatim at the stated place in the held Rosetta PDF (read as a 200-dpi page image, not just scanned); the p.8 kag/a~kaga notation pair and the p.9-10 'l'accent porte sur la première voyelle' passage are also confirmed; the Stevenson typescript's tri-tonal statement (p.16) and absence of any stress section are confirmed. (2) Deciding source: a 1909 colonial grammar sketch. It is NOT the best available description of Bagirmi prosody — Stevenson 1969 (205-pp reference grammar) and Keegan & Djibrine 2016 (held, 294 pp) are — but both later works describe tone only and are silent on stress, so for the narrow question 'is there a fixed stress pattern' the record's exit is safe and the StressTyp2 'final stress' contradiction note is justified (StressTyp2's gloss 'The final vowel is the stressed one' over-reads Gaden's

sources.quote: Gaden 1909:9: "When a word occurs inside a clause, or in a compound, or carries a suffix, if the accent does not fall on its final vowel, that vowel disappears... If, on the contrary, the accent falls on the final vowel, the word undergoes no alteration." and "If one considers words of the kag/a type, in which the accent falls on the first vowel, one notices that in the majority of cases the final vowel is the same as the accented vowel." (The Stevenson quote is English.)
